essentials: The Green Claims Directive is a **proposal, not law**. It would require companies to **substantiate and have verified** explicit environmental claims before using them.
It was designed as the companion to the ECGT: the ECGT bans the worst practices, the Green Claims Directive would set the standard of proof for the rest.
Negotiations have been **on hold since June 2025**, when the Commission announced it intended to withdraw the proposal and the final trilogue was cancelled.
Companies should **not plan on it**, but its content shows what good substantiation looks like and what courts may expect anyway.

sections.title: Why it was proposed
text: Banning generic claims leaves a question open: when exactly is a specific claim, such as ‘30% less CO2 than the previous model’, sufficiently proven? Today that is decided case by case under the general rules on misleading practices, with different outcomes across Member States. In March 2023 the Commission proposed common minimum requirements and, more controversially, a check before the claim is made.

sections.title: What the proposal contains
points: **Substantiation.** An explicit environmental claim would have to rest on an assessment using recognised scientific evidence, taking a life-cycle perspective, covering all significant environmental aspects, and showing that the claimed benefit goes beyond legal requirements and does not shift harm elsewhere.
**Verification before use.** An independent accredited verifier would check the claim and issue a certificate of conformity recognised across the EU.
**Communication.** Claims would have to come with accessible information on the substantiation, for example through a link or QR code.
**Comparative claims.** Comparisons would need equivalent data and methods for the products compared.
**Climate claims.** Greater transparency about the use of offsets and the split between own reductions and compensation.
**Labelling schemes.** New private schemes would be allowed only if they add value over existing ones; schemes would need transparent governance and independent verification.
**Penalties.** Fines of up to at least 4% of annual turnover, confiscation of revenue and exclusion from public procurement.

sections.title: How the procedure stalled
steps: **June 2025**: days before what was planned as the final trilogue, the Commission states that it intends to withdraw the proposal, pointing to the burden on micro-enterprises. The meeting is cancelled and the Council presidency loses its majority for a mandate.
**Since then**: the proposal has neither been formally withdrawn nor taken up again.

sections.title: The sticking points
points: **Micro-enterprises.** Whether companies with fewer than ten employees should be covered was the immediate cause of the breakdown. Around 30 million micro-enterprises would have been affected.
**Ex-ante verification.** Having every claim certified in advance was seen by many as too costly and slow; a simplified procedure for some claims was discussed.
**The political climate.** The file collided with the simplification agenda that produced the Omnibus packages.

sections.title: What applies in the meantime
text: Environmental claims are far from unregulated. The **ECGT** bans generic claims, unverified labels and offset-based product claims since September 2026. The general prohibition of misleading practices requires any factual claim to be correct and provable, and authorities and courts in several Member States have taken action against greenwashing on that basis. In effect, the trader must be able to substantiate a claim when challenged; what is missing is only the uniform method and the check in advance.

mistakes.wrong: The Green Claims Directive is in force.
mistakes.right: It is an unadopted proposal, on hold since June 2025.

mistakes.wrong: Because it stalled, green claims are unregulated.
mistakes.right: The ECGT and the general rules on misleading practices apply, and claims must be provable when challenged.

mistakes.wrong: The ECGT and the Green Claims Directive are the same act.
mistakes.right: The ECGT is adopted and bans specific practices. The Green Claims proposal would add substantiation and verification rules.

mistakes.wrong: The proposal has been formally withdrawn.
mistakes.right: The Commission announced its intention. As long as it is not withdrawn, negotiations could in theory resume.

practice: **Comply with the ECGT** first; that is binding law.
**Keep a substantiation file** for every specific claim: data, method, scope, date. It is your defence under current law.
Use the proposal's criteria as a **quality check**: life-cycle view, significant aspects, no trade-offs, beyond legal requirements.
**Watch the tracker** for any restart or formal withdrawal.
**Follow national practice**: consumer authorities and courts already set the bar in individual cases.

quiz.q: What is the legal status of the Green Claims Directive?
options: A proposal on hold since June 2025
quiz.why: It was proposed in March 2023 and never adopted. The final trilogue in June 2025 was cancelled.

quiz.q: What would the proposal have added to the ECGT?
options: A ban on all environmental claims
Requirements to substantiate claims and have them verified before use
Mandatory use of the EU Ecolabel
quiz.why: Its core is a minimum standard of substantiation plus ex-ante verification by an accredited verifier.

quiz.q: Which issue triggered the breakdown of negotiations in June 2025?
options: The level of the carbon price
quiz.why: The Commission cited the burden on micro-enterprises when it announced its intention to withdraw the proposal.

quiz.q: A company makes a specific claim: ‘40% recycled plastic’. The Green Claims Directive is stalled. What applies?
options: The claim must still be true and provable under the rules on misleading practices
The claim is banned under the ECGT
The claim needs approval by the Commission
quiz.why: Specific claims are allowed but must be accurate, and the trader has to be able to prove them when challenged.

options: Verification by an independent body before the claim is used
quiz.why: Ex ante means beforehand. It was one of the most contested elements because of cost and delay.

quiz.q: In which stage of the tracker is the file?
quiz.why: Both co-legislators adopted positions and trilogues began, so it reached the negotiating stage before it stalled.
